Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Layla describes her life before the accident as one of quiet competence, defined by the solitary rhythms of the forest. Six months ago, that changed. She was driving her work truck back from a timber survey on a winding, two-lane road at dusk. Coming around a sharp bend, she was confronted by the immediate aftermath of a collision. A sedan had swerved to avoid a deer and hit an old-growth oak. The scene is not a linear story in her mind but a series of sensory fragments. She remembers the hiss of the radiator, the surreal stillness of the deer’s body on the asphalt, and the sharp, coppery smell of blood mixed with leaking gasoline. Through the shattered windshield, she could see the driver, a man, slumped against the steering wheel. In that moment, Layla froze. She, who prided herself on being practical and decisive in emergencies, simply stood by her truck, her boots feeling fused to the pavement, until another car finally arrived and its driver called 911.

In the months since, the memory has been a persistent, unwelcome visitor. It never plays out in full; she finds herself pushing it away, a mental flinching, just before the wave of shame about her inaction can crest. When she does recall it, the experience is strangely distant, as if she is watching a distressing scene from a film that has nothing to do with her. The memory feels like it belongs to someone else, a more cowardly and ineffectual version of herself. Yet, its sensory details remain brutally vivid. While marking trees deep in a stand of pines, far from any road, she will suddenly be overwhelmed by the distinct smell of hot metal and gasoline, a phantom scent that brings the panic of that evening rushing back.

Her work, once a source of peace, has become a landscape of potential threats. Driving the narrow access roads to job sites is an exercise in tension. Her eyes constantly dart from the road to the tree line and back again, scanning for any sign of movement, any glint of metal through the leaves. She has come to believe that danger is everywhere, and it is her sole responsibility to anticipate it. This constant vigilance is exhausting. Back at the forestry station, the casual chatter of her colleagues can feel like a minefield. Any discussion of car trouble or near-misses on the highway sends a jolt of anxiety through her. She will abruptly leave the room, making an excuse about needing to check her equipment, rather than endure listening to a story that might involve an accident. This has created a distance between her and her team, who now see her as aloof and unpredictable.

A profound sense of self-blame has taken root. Layla is certain that she failed in a moment of critical importance. The thought "I should have protected him" runs on a loop, a constant internal flagellation. She feels she acted in a way that goes against her most fundamental values of courage and responsibility. This belief has poisoned her self-perception, draining the joy from her life. She looks back at the person she was six months ago—happy, confident, at home in the world—and sees a stranger. Now, she feels only a persistent, heavy misery. To escape the thoughts that crowd in during the quiet of the evening, she has begun staying up until two or three in the morning, scrolling through her phone until she collapses from sheer exhaustion, hoping to fall asleep too quickly to dream. It was after she snapped at a coworker for mentioning a minor fender-bender in the parking lot that she finally made an appointment. The shocked look on his face made her realize how unrecognizable she had become, not just to herself, but to others. She is seeking help because she cannot bear to be this miserable, frightened person anymore, but she is terrified that getting better will mean having to fully remember and accept the version of herself that stood frozen on the roadside, watching.
